notes: Already in OpenLoco catalog. Excellent reference for the wheeled-balancing morphology gap.
prior_art_notes: Upkie demonstrates fully-open wheeled-bipedal balancing using commodity mjbots actuators. Anticipates cost-effective wheeled-humanoid designs.
sources: Caron, S. publications and project documentation.

actuator_details: Series-elastic actuators in legs; direct-drive wheels

creator: ETH Zurich, RSL

notes: ETH RSL has spun out commercial Ascento entity.
prior_art_notes: Ascento is foundational prior art for wheeled-bipedal-with-jumping morphology. Anticipates designs combining wheeled efficiency with leg-based obstacle traversal.

actuator_details: Torque-controlled actuators
control_architecture: Master Maneuvering System teleoperation with force feedback
creator: Toyota Motor Corporation Partner Robot Division
disclosure_citation: Toyota Motor Corporation public reveal, November 2017.

prior_art_notes: T-HR3 is significant prior art for whole-body teleoperated humanoids with force feedback. The Master Maneuvering System teleoperation interface anticipates many modern humanoid teleop claims.

actuator_details: Open BLDC motor controller with field-oriented control

creator: ODrive Robotics
disclosure_citation: Sirkin, Oskar. ODrive open hardware release, 2017.

prior_art_notes: ODrive is significant prior art for open BLDC controller designs. Has been used in countless academic and hobbyist robotics projects since 2017.

actuator_details: Open BLDC controller optimized for QDD robotics applications; CAN-FD

prior_art_notes: mjbots Moteus is foundational prior art for compact open BLDC controllers in legged robotics. Used in Berkeley Humanoid, Upkie, and many academic platforms.

actuator_details: Open Arduino-compatible FOC library for BLDC and stepper motors
control_architecture: FOC, position/velocity/torque
creator: SimpleFOC community
disclosure_citation: Skuric, Antun et al. SimpleFOC library release, 2020.

actuator_details: Standard Spot electric actuators
control_architecture: Spot stock control stack
creator: Boston Dynamics
disclosure_citation: Boston Dynamics partnership announcements with fuel cell vendors, 2020.
ip_citations: Boston Dynamics patents on Spot platform
notes: Variant entry rather than full Spot lineage; covers the power-fuel-cell taxonomy gap.
prior_art_notes: Demonstrates fuel-cell-powered legged robotics at commercial scale. Anticipates fuel-cell power claims in field robotics applications.

actuator_details: Custom electric actuators including cycloidal reducers in some joints

creator: Unitree Robotics
disclosure_citation: Unitree Robotics G1 reveal, May 2024.

actuator_details: Robotis Dynamixel servos

creator: Robotis Co. with University of Pennsylvania, Virginia Tech, Purdue

notes: Major influence on the educational/research humanoid space.
prior_art_notes: DARwIn-OP is foundational prior art for fully-open small-scale humanoid platforms. Predates Poppy by several years for the academic-open category.

actuator_details: Custom electric actuators with brushed and brushless motors
control_architecture: NAOqi middleware; behavior trees and learned components

sensing: cameras, microphones, IMU, sonars, force-sensing resistors

actuator_details: Custom electric actuators
control_architecture: NAOqi middleware; emotion engine

disclosure_citation: SoftBank Robotics public reveal of Pepper, June 2014.

prior_art_notes: Pepper is foundational prior art for wheeled-base humanoid social robots. The omnidirectional wheeled base design has been widely cited.
sensing: cameras, microphones, IMU, lasers, sonars, tactile

actuator_details: Custom electric actuators with series-elastic in some joints

creator: Willow Garage
disclosure_citation: Willow Garage. PR2 platform release, 2010.

notes: Willow Garage is defunct but PR2's influence persists through ROS, MoveIt, and the broad community. Several PR2 units remain in academic operation.
prior_art_notes: PR2 was the platform around which ROS was originally built. Its hardware is significant prior art for omnidirectional wheeled mobile manipulation. ROS itself is even more significant prior art for robotics middleware.
sensing: stereo cameras, LiDAR, force-torque, tilting laser
sources: Quigley, M. et al. 'ROS: an open-source Robot Operating System.' ICRA Workshop 2009.

actuator_details: Multiple platforms; not platform-specific
control_architecture: VLA model with flow-matching policy head
creator: Physical Intelligence
disclosure_citation: Black, K. et al. 'π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control.' arXiv 2410.24164, October 2024.
ip_citations: arXiv preprint discloses architecture; weights and dataset proprietary
notes: Software/policy entry rather than embodiment entry; exists across many platforms.
prior_art_notes: π0 paper discloses VLA-with-flow-matching architecture publicly. The arXiv preprint is itself prior art for that specific architectural pattern.

actuator_details: control architecture, not embodied
control_architecture: Simplex: high-assurance simple controller with verified safety envelope, alongside complex high-performance controller, with a decision module that switches to the simple controller when complex controller violates envelope
creator: Lui Sha, Carnegie Mellon University
disclosure_citation: Sha, Lui. 'Dependable system upgrade.' Proceedings 19th IEEE Real-Time Systems Symposium, 1998. Earlier conceptual work circa 1995.
ip_citations: academic publication; concept widely adopted without IP enforcement
notable_capabilities: formal safety guarantees in presence of complex/unverified control
backbone of much modern safety-critical control
notes: Simplex is among the most-cited safety architecture concepts in real-time and cyber-physical systems literature.
prior_art_notes: Foundational prior art for safety supervisor architectures in robotics and physical AI. Any 'safety supervisor' or 'safety envelope' or 'fallback controller' patent claim post-1995 must contend with Sha's Simplex work as anticipating prior art. Directly relevant to MathGround's Simplex supervisor architecture.
sources: Sha, L. 'Using Simplicity to Control Complexity.' IEEE Software 18(4), 2001.
Crenshaw, T.L. et al. 'The Simplex reference model: limiting fault-propagation due to unreliable components in cyber-physical system architectures.' RTSS 2007.

actuator_details: control architecture
control_architecture: Runtime monitor that switches between primary and verified backup controller based on safety constraint satisfaction
creator: Air Force Research Laboratory and DARPA program
disclosure_citation: Schierman, J.D. et al. 'Runtime Assurance Framework Development for Highly Adaptive Flight Control Systems.' Air Force Research Laboratory, 2015. Earlier DARPA AACUS work circa 2010.
ip_citations: AFRL technical reports; DARPA-funded; broadly published
notable_capabilities: enables fielding of unverified ML-based controllers in safety-critical aviation
notes: AFRL RTA work is widely cited but underappreciated outside aerospace. Worth surfacing in robotics-domain prior art arguments.
prior_art_notes: Direct descendant of Simplex; the 'unverified neural net plus verified safety controller' pattern. Anticipates modern ML-safety supervisor patents in autonomous vehicles, drones, and robotics. Directly applicable as prior art to safety claims in physical AI products.

actuator_details: mathematical control framework
control_architecture: Lyapunov-like functions that certify forward invariance of a safe set under a control law; can be composed with QP-based controllers for online safety filtering
creator: Peter Wieland and Frank Allgöwer (early formalization); Aaron Ames and others (modern formalization)
disclosure_citation: Wieland, P. and Allgöwer, F. 'Constructive safety using control barrier functions.' IFAC Proceedings Volumes 40(12), 2007.
notable_capabilities: composable with arbitrary nominal controllers via QP
applied across robotics, vehicles, multi-agent systems
notes: The Ames 2017 paper is the most-cited modern reference; the Wieland 2007 paper is the deeper prior art origin.
prior_art_notes: CBFs are the dominant modern formalism for online safety filtering in robotics. Substantial prior art for any patent claiming online safety filtering, safety-aware QP control, or formally-bounded safe ML execution. Particularly relevant to MathGround's Universal Fuzz Law work as the formal foundation for safety envelopes.
sources: Wieland, P. and Allgöwer, F. IFAC 2007.
Ames, A.D. et al. 'Control Barrier Function Based Quadratic Programs for Safety Critical Systems.' IEEE TAC 62(8), 2017.
Ames, A.D. et al. 'Control Barrier Functions: Theory and Applications.' ECC 2019.

actuator_details: as positronic robots
control_architecture: Adds 'A robot may not harm humanity, or, by inaction, allow humanity to come to harm' as priority-zero rule, restructuring the Three Laws priority order
creator: Isaac Asimov
disclosure_citation: Asimov, Isaac. Robots and Empire. Doubleday, 1985.
notable_capabilities: tradeoff between individual harm and collective benefit
notes: Pairs with the original Three Laws entry to provide a more complete picture of fictional priority-ordered safety architectures.
prior_art_notes: Significant for safety architecture prior art because it explicitly demonstrates priority-reordering in a hard-constraint hierarchy under conflicting goals. Anticipates modern AI safety frameworks dealing with population-scale or systemic harm tradeoffs.

actuator_details: safety standard
control_architecture: Defines speed and separation monitoring, power and force limiting, hand guiding, safety-rated monitored stop
creator: ISO TC 299 (Robotics) working group
disclosure_citation: ISO 10218-1:2006 'Robots and robotic devices — Safety requirements for industrial robots — Part 1: Robots.' International Organization for Standardization.
notable_capabilities: industry-standard safety modes for collaborative robots
categorical safety requirements for power-and-force-limited operation
notes: Including standards documents in the corpus is a deliberate choice: they are publicly disclosed, dated, and constitute defensive prior art for claims in their domain.
prior_art_notes: ISO 10218 (and the related ISO/TS 15066 for collaborative operation) constitute foundational prior art for collaborative robot safety claims. Any patent claim around 'safety-rated monitored stop,' 'speed and separation monitoring,' or 'power and force limiting' in collaborative robotics is anticipated by these standards.

actuator_details: safety analysis framework
control_architecture: Computes backward-reachable sets representing states from which a safety-violating state can be forced by adversary inputs; produces verified safe controllers
creator: Ian Mitchell, Alexandre Bayen, Claire Tomlin (UC Berkeley/Stanford)
disclosure_citation: Mitchell, I.M., Bayen, A.M., Tomlin, C.J. 'A time-dependent Hamilton-Jacobi formulation of reachable sets for continuous dynamic games.' IEEE TAC 50(7), 2005.
notable_capabilities: formally verified safety in continuous nonlinear systems
notes: Tomlin's group at UCB has been the most prolific source of HJ reachability applications.
prior_art_notes: Foundational prior art for formally-verified safe control. Any patent claiming 'verified safety envelopes' or 'formal safety guarantees' for autonomous systems must contend with HJ reachability work.
sources: Mitchell, I.M. et al. IEEE TAC 50(7), 2005.
Bansal, S. et al. 'Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability: A Brief Overview and Recent Advances.' CDC 2017.

actuator_details: learning algorithm safety wrapper
control_architecture: Synthesized reactive shield monitors RL agent actions and overrides any action that could violate temporal-logic safety specification
creator: Mohammed Alshiekh, Roderick Bloem, Rüdiger Ehlers, Bettina Könighofer, Scott Niekum, Ufuk Topcu
disclosure_citation: Alshiekh, M. et al. 'Safe Reinforcement Learning via Shielding.' AAAI 2018.
notable_capabilities: formal safety guarantees during RL training and deployment
temporal logic specification of safety properties
notes: Particularly relevant to physical AI deployment patents where ML-based control is wrapped in formal safety mechanisms.
prior_art_notes: Major prior art for any patent on RL safety filtering, shielded ML, or temporal-logic-bounded RL. Combined with Simplex and CBF prior art, makes much of the 'safe ML' patent space difficult to defend.
sources: Subsequent work by Könighofer, Bloem, others.

actuator_details: Harmonic-drive electric actuators throughout
control_architecture: ZMP-based with stretched-knee gait
creator: Waseda University, Takanishi Laboratory
disclosure_citation: Ogura, Y. et al. 'Development of a New Humanoid Robot WABIAN-2.' ICRA 2006.
notable_capabilities: designed as a human walking research platform
notes: Continues the Waseda lineage from WABOT-1. WABIAN-2R is a refined variant.
prior_art_notes: WABIAN-2's stretched-knee gait disclosure is significant prior art for any humanoid walking control claim aiming at more human-like locomotion (less crouched, more upright knees during stance). Distinct from ASIMO's bent-knee paradigm. The Takanishi laboratory's continued publication makes this a well-anchored academic disclosure.

actuator_details: Electric servo actuators

creator: Honda Motor Co.
disclosure_citation: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. 'Honda humanoid robots development.' Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).

prior_art_notes: Step in the Honda E-series lineage. Hirose/Ogawa 2007 documents the entire E0–E6 progression with sufficient specificity to anticipate basic electric-actuated bipedal walking claims for that era.
sources: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).

actuator_details: Electric servos

creator: Honda Motor Co.

ip_citations: Hirose/Ogawa 2007 Phil Trans paper retrospective disclosure

sources: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).

actuator_details: Electric servos

creator: Honda Motor Co.
disclosure_citation: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. 'Honda humanoid robots development.' Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).

sources: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).

actuator_details: Electric servos with knee bending

actuator_details: Electric servos; first untethered model in series

actuator_details: Electric servos with active stair-climbing capability

prior_art_notes: Final E-series model before transition to P-series. Relevant to bipedal stair-climbing claims.

actuator_details: First Honda humanoid with arms in addition to legs
control_architecture: whole-body coordination, separate from previous legs-only platforms
creator: Honda Motor Co.
disclosure_citation: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. 'Honda humanoid robots development.' Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).
notable_capabilities: first full-humanoid (legs + arms + torso) in Honda lineage
notes: P2 (1996) and P3 (1997) follow before ASIMO (2000); covered separately in next pass.
prior_art_notes: Transition from legs-only to full humanoid in the Honda lineage. P1 is the architectural ancestor of ASIMO. Anticipates subsequent claims around full-humanoid actuated platforms with arms and legs.
sources: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).

actuator_details: Harmonic-drive electric servos
control_architecture: ZMP-based dynamic balancing; first published Honda ZMP work
creator: Honda Motor Co.
disclosure_citation: Honda Motor Co. press release, December 20, 1996, Tokyo. Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).
ip_citations: Honda patents on bipedal control filed late 1990s; many now expired
notable_capabilities: public reveal shocked humanoid robotics community
notes: Hirai et al. ICRA 1998 is the definitive academic disclosure of P2's design. Among the highest-value commons entries because it predates and anticipates so much.
prior_art_notes: P2's December 1996 reveal is among the most significant single events in humanoid robotics history. Honda's ZMP-based dynamic balancing as publicly disclosed via P2 anticipates virtually all subsequent commercial bipedal locomotion claims using ZMP. Honda's 1990s patent filings, many of which have now expired, form the deepest commercial prior art chain in the field.
sources: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).
Hirai, K. et al. 'The development of Honda humanoid robot.' ICRA 1998.

actuator_details: Harmonic-drive electric servos; magnesium-alloy frame for weight reduction
control_architecture: refined ZMP-based dynamic balancing
creator: Honda Motor Co.
disclosure_citation: Honda Motor Co. press materials, September 1997. Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).
notable_capabilities: lighter and more agile than P2
prior_art_notes: Final Honda P-series prototype before ASIMO. Refinements to the P2 architecture; key continuity in the Honda prior art chain.
sources: Hirose, M. and Ogawa, K. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 365, 11–19 (2007).

actuator_details: Harmonic-drive electric servos with dust/water resistance

actuator_details: Lightweight harmonic-drive servos
control_architecture: ZMP-based
creator: AIST and Kawada Industries
disclosure_citation: Kaneko, K. et al. 'Humanoid Robot HRP-4: Humanoid Robotics Platform with Lightweight and Slim Body.' IROS 2010.
notes: HRP-4C (separate variant, focused on female-form humanoid for entertainment) is a related but distinct entry not included here.
prior_art_notes: HRP-4 lightweight design anticipates subsequent slim-form humanoid claims. The 2010 IROS paper provides full mechanical specifications openly.

actuator_details: High-power harmonic-drive servos with wide range of motion
control_architecture: whole-body multi-contact motion planning
creator: AIST and Kawada Industries
disclosure_citation: Kaneko, K. et al. 'Humanoid Robot HRP-5P: An Electrically Actuated Humanoid Robot With High-Power and Wide-Range Joints.' IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 4(2), 2019.
notes: Continues the HRP series' uninterrupted open-academic disclosure tradition.

sources: Kaneko, K. et al. IEEE RA-L 4(2), 2019.

actuator_details: Custom electric actuators; Figure-claimed 50% torque-density improvement over Figure 01

creator: Figure AI

sources: Figure AI website and demonstration videos.

actuator_details: Series-elastic actuators with fiberglass leaf-spring legs implementing the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model
control_architecture: reduced-order spring-mass model; SLIP-based control
creator: Oregon State University, Dynamic Robotics Laboratory (Jonathan Hurst)
disclosure_citation: Hubicki, C. et al. 'ATRIAS: Design and validation of a tether-free 3D-capable spring-mass bipedal robot.' International Journal of Robotics Research 35(12), 2016.
ip_citations: academic publication; OSU patents licensed widely
notable_capabilities: first machine to walk in 3D space using passive-dynamics-inspired control
demonstrated robust unscripted human-like walking gaits
notes: Direct ancestor of Cassie which became the basis for Agility Robotics' Digit. The Hurst-lab academic chain is among the most-cited in modern bipedal robotics.
prior_art_notes: ATRIAS is foundational prior art for spring-mass bipedal locomotion. The SLIP-based reduced-order control approach has become a dominant paradigm in dynamic bipedal walking, anticipating many subsequent commercial control claims.
sources: Hurst, J. et al. various IROS and ICRA publications, 2012-2015.

actuator_details: Quasi-direct-drive proprioceptive actuators (foundational implementation)
control_architecture: impulse-based bounding control
creator: MIT Biomimetic Robotics Lab (Sangbae Kim)
disclosure_citation: Park, H.-W. et al. 'High-speed bounding with the MIT Cheetah 2: Control design and experiments.' International Journal of Robotics Research 36(2), 2017. Earlier ICRA disclosure 2014.
ip_citations: MIT academic publications; Wensing 2017 T-RO paper on actuator design
notes: Original MIT Cheetah (1) was hydraulic; Cheetah 2 transitioned to electric QDD which became the architectural standard.
prior_art_notes: MIT Cheetah 2 establishes the QDD actuator topology in a working high-speed legged robot. The Wensing 2017 T-RO paper 'Proprioceptive actuator design in the MIT Cheetah' is the foundational actuator design disclosure.
sources: Wensing, P.M. et al. 'Proprioceptive actuator design in the MIT Cheetah.' IEEE T-RO 33(3), 2017.

actuator_details: Refined QDD actuators
control_architecture: convex MPC; blind locomotion (no vision)
creator: MIT Biomimetic Robotics Lab (Sangbae Kim)
disclosure_citation: Bledt, G. et al. 'MIT Cheetah 3: Design and Control of a Robust, Dynamic Quadruped Robot.' IROS 2018.
notes: Cheetah 3 was directly downscaled into the Mini Cheetah platform.
prior_art_notes: Cheetah 3 establishes blind robust legged locomotion using only proprioceptive sensing — a significant prior art point against later vision-dependent legged-robot claims.

actuator_details: Custom QDD actuators, derived from MIT Cheetah-style design

creator: Unitree Robotics

notes: Go1 is the most-deployed Unitree platform and the immediate predecessor to the H1 humanoid architecture.
prior_art_notes: Unitree Go1 actuator design is heavily anticipated by MIT Cheetah QDD prior art (Wensing 2017, Katz 2019). Pricing-driven commodification rather than novel IP.

actuator_details: Pre-WWII-developed giant humanoid weapon platform; remote-controlled by handheld console

The remote-control rather than piloted-cockpit architecture is a notable structural distinction from later mecha (Mazinger, Gundam) where the operator is inside.

(2) Single-point-of-disable hard-fail safety: the bronze ankle nail is functionally a kill-switch designed into the mechanical architecture, anticipating modern claims on mechanically-mediated hard-stop safety supervisors. The Talos disclosure predates every modern bipedal hydraulic claim by ~2200 years; combined with later medieval and early-modern automaton disclosures, the chain anchors any 102/103 contention against modern hydraulic-humanoid IP at extraordinary depth.

Modern claims on cable-driven anthropomorphic hands or tendon-routed humanoid actuators face an extraordinarily deep 102 anchor here. The Codex Atlanticus is publicly held (Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Milan) and has been continuously cited since the 19th century.

The companion automata (The Musician with breathing motion, The Draughtsman with multiple drawings) extend this disclosure to keyboard playing and pencil sketching. Continuously exhibited since 1774; documented in Chapuis-Droz 1958 (the canonical reference).

prior_art_notes: Foundational fictional disclosure of a hard-constraint safety supervisor implemented as the highest-priority directive in a distributed humanoid fleet. Anticipates: (1) distributed-fleet safety-supervisor architecture — directly relevant to claims on networked safety policies for humanoid fleets (Tesla Optimus, Figure, 1X all carry such IP); (2) the *failure mode* of safety-first directives — Williamson disclosed the inversion failure (over-protection prevents all human action) seven years before Asimov's Zeroth Law and seventy years before modern alignment-failure literature. Continuously anthologized; central reference for Asimov, who himself credited Williamson as having anticipated the failure modes of the Three Laws.

actuator_details: Four-legged hydraulic walking machine, 1400 kg dry mass, 1500 kg payload capacity, 5.5m long. Each leg has 3 hydraulic cylinders for rotation/extension/elevation. Driven by 90 hp Continental gasoline engine driving hydraulic pump.
control_architecture: master-slave kinesthetic teleoperation: human operator's arms and legs are strapped into kinesthetic-feedback exoskeleton; force-reflecting servo couples operator joint position/torque to vehicle leg position/torque; operator feels the vehicle's interaction forces
creator: Ralph S. Mosher and team, General Electric Research Laboratory, Schenectady NY
disclosure_citation: Mosher, Ralph S. 'Test and evaluation of a versatile walking truck.' General Electric Schenectady Research Lab Report, September 1968. Published abstract: Mosher, R.S. 'Exploring the potential of a quadruped'. Society of Automotive Engineers, January 1969 (Detroit Engineering Show, Paper 690191).
notable_capabilities: hydraulic legged locomotion at 1500 kg payload
master-slave kinesthetic control with force feedback
prior_art_notes: The GE Walking Truck is the deepest hydraulic legged-locomotion academic disclosure in the corpus and substantially predates everything in the modern legged-robotics commercial portfolio. Mosher's 1968 SAE paper discloses with full specificity: (1) hydraulic actuation per leg with 3-DOF — anticipates hydraulic legged claims by Boston Dynamics (BigDog 2005) by 37 years; (2) master-slave kinesthetic teleoperation with force feedback — anticipates teleoperation claims for legged systems; (3) 1500 kg payload legged loadbearing — anticipates legged-loadbearing claims (Boston Dynamics LS3, Ghost Robotics Vision 60); (4) 90 hp combustion engine power source for legged locomotion. Modern claims on hydraulic / combustion-powered legged loadbearing all face this 1968 disclosure as 102 prior art at unusual depth. Publicly funded research, openly published.
sensing: force feedback at every joint; visual via operator's direct view; no autonomous sensing
sources: Mosher, R.S. 'Exploring the potential of a quadruped'. SAE Paper 690191, 1969.
Mosher, R.S. 'Test and evaluation of a versatile walking truck'. GE Schenectady Research Lab Report, 1968.
Liston, R. and Mosher, R. 'A versatile walking truck'. Mechanical Engineering 90(8): 12-19, 1968.

actuator_details: Single pneumatic-piston leg with hip joint for fore-aft balance; planar (2D) constrained motion. Pneumatic spring leg with active hip-position control. The leg compresses on landing and extends to provide thrust.
control_architecture: three-part decoupled control: (1) hopping height regulated by leg-spring extension during stance; (2) forward velocity regulated by foot-placement during flight; (3) body attitude regulated by hip torque. The decoupling is the disclosure.
creator: Marc H. Raibert; CMU Leg Laboratory, then MIT Leg Laboratory
disclosure_citation: Raibert, Marc H. 'Hopping in legged systems — modeling and simulation for the two-dimensional one-legged case'. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics SMC-14(3): 451-463, May/June 1984. Earlier: Raibert, M.H. and Brown, H.B. 'Experiments in balance with a 2D one-legged machine'. Trans. ASME, J. Dyn. Sys., Meas., Cont., 106:75-81, 1984.
notable_capabilities: dynamic legged balance via decoupled three-axis control
experimental validation of dynamic legged stability
prior_art_notes: Raibert's hoppers are the foundational academic disclosure of dynamic legged balance and reduced-order-model control. The three-part decoupling (leg height / foot placement / body attitude) is the *exact* control architecture used by every subsequent dynamic-legged academic and commercial system, from Cassie to Atlas to MIT Mini Cheetah. Modern claims on reduced-order-model legged control all face Raibert's 1984 disclosure as 102 prior art. The 1985 book (Legged Robots that Balance, MIT Press) extends the disclosure to 2-legged and 4-legged versions and is one of the most-cited works in legged robotics. Publicly funded research; open publication.
sensing: leg position encoder; body pitch encoder; ground contact sensor
sources: Raibert, M.H. 'Hopping in legged systems'. IEEE Trans. SMC, 1984.
Raibert, M.H. and Brown, H.B. 'Experiments in balance with a 2D one-legged machine'. ASME J. DSMC, 1984.
Raibert, M.H. Legged Robots that Balance. MIT Press, 1986.

actuator_details: Unactuated bipedal mechanism. Knee-locked stance leg + free-swinging swing leg. Hip joint between legs. Walks down a shallow incline on gravity alone, no motors, no batteries, no sensors, no controller.
control_architecture: zero — purely passive mechanical dynamics. The walker's natural limit cycle on a slope produces stable bipedal locomotion. Stability arises from the dynamics, not from feedback.
creator: Tad McGeer, Simon Fraser University
disclosure_citation: McGeer, Tad. 'Passive dynamic walking'. International Journal of Robotics Research 9(2): 62-82, April 1990.
prior_art_notes: The 1990 McGeer disclosure is the foundational academic anchor for energy-efficient bipedal locomotion. Anticipates: (1) the principle that bipedal stability can emerge from passive limb dynamics (with appropriate inertia/length tuning) — directly relevant to modern claims on energy-efficient bipedal control IP; (2) limit-cycle analysis of bipedal gait — anticipates analytical claims on cycle-based gait optimization; (3) the methodological observation that the cost of transport for passive walkers approaches that of human walking. Modern energy-efficient bipedal claims (Cassie, ATRIAS, Berkeley Humanoid) all build on McGeer 1990. Publicly funded research; the 1990 IJRR paper is heavily cited.
sources: Collins, S.H., Wisse, M., Ruina, A. 'A three-dimensional passive-dynamic walking robot with two legs and knees'. IJRR 20(7): 607-615, 2001 (extends McGeer to 3D).

control_architecture: position and force control modes; tendon-tension control via per-actuator solenoids
creator: Shadow Robot Company (Richard Greenhill, Rich Walker, et al.)
disclosure_citation: Greenhill, Richard et al. (Shadow Robot Company). 'Shadow Dexterous Hand'. ICRA workshops 2002 onwards; mechanical disclosures in Greenhill, R., Walker, R. et al. 'The Shadow C5 Hand Prototype'. ICRA Workshop on Humanoid Manipulation, 2007.
end_effector: five-fingered anthropomorphic hand at human scale
prior_art_notes: Shadow's hand is the longest-running academic-grade dexterous hand platform and is the standard reference for tendon-routed anthropomorphic manipulators. Anticipates and provides extensive prior art for: (1) 24-DOF anthropomorphic hand mechanism with separate-finger control — relevant to modern humanoid hand IP; (2) McKibben-style pneumatic muscle actuation in a hand — relevant to artificial-muscle hand claims; (3) tendon-tension control as a viable closed-loop mode for dexterity — relevant to tendon-controlled hand IP. Shadow has published extensively in IEEE proceedings since 2002, and the platform is licensed to academic labs worldwide. Modern Tesla, Figure, and 1X hand patents face Shadow's 22+ years of accumulated public disclosure.
sensing: strain gauges in tendon paths; fingertip pressure sensors; joint encoders
sources: Shadow Robot Company. 'Shadow C5 Hand'. ICRA Workshop on Humanoid Manipulation, 2007.
Shadow Robot Company. Shadow Dexterous Hand technical specification (publicly distributed).

actuator_details: Four-fingered hand, 13 DOF (3 per finger + 1 palm rotation). Brushless DC motors with harmonic-drive reducers. Cable-tendon transmission to phalanges. Joint torque sensing at every actuated joint. Force-torque sensor at fingertip.
control_architecture: impedance control via measured joint torques; backdrivable; supports Cartesian and joint-space control modes
creator: Butterfass, Grebenstein, Liu, Hirzinger; DLR Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics, Oberpfaffenhofen, Germany
disclosure_citation: Butterfass, J., Grebenstein, M., Liu, H., Hirzinger, G. 'DLR-Hand II: next generation of a dextrous robot hand'. IEEE ICRA, 2001 (early disclosure); Butterfass, J. et al. 'Design and Experiences with DLR Hand II'. World Automation Congress, 2004.
end_effector: four-fingered hand with thumb opposition; human-equivalent grasp envelope
notable_capabilities: compact integration of motors+sensors per joint
prior_art_notes: DLR Hand-II is the canonical academic disclosure of joint-torque-sensing dexterous hands with compact actuator integration. Anticipates: (1) impedance-controlled dexterous manipulation with proprioceptive sensing — directly relevant to claims on torque-controlled humanoid hands (every modern humanoid hand IP); (2) cable-tendon transmission with harmonic-drive primary reducer — relevant to combined-mechanism actuator claims; (3) per-joint integrated torque sensor with calibrated absolute position — anticipates proprioceptive-actuator IP. The DLR series (Hand-II, then Hand-III, then Hand Arm System) is one of the deepest academic technical lineages in dexterous manipulation. Continuously published in IEEE proceedings since 2001.
sensing: joint torque sensors at every joint; six-axis force-torque at fingertip; joint position encoders; absolute calibration via Hall sensors
sources: Butterfass, J. et al. 'DLR-Hand II: next generation of a dextrous robot hand'. IEEE ICRA 2001.
Butterfass, J. et al. 'Design and Experiences with DLR Hand II'. World Automation Congress 2004.

actuator_details: Wheeled humanoid: omnidirectional 4-wheel base with variable wheel-base width for stability/agility tradeoff. Two DLR LWR (Light Weight Robot) arms (7 DOF each). Two DLR Hand-II four-finger hands. Sensorized head with stereo cameras and structured light.
control_architecture: impedance control on the arms; coordinated whole-body motion planning; mobile manipulation tasks (catching balls, pouring, two-arm manipulation)
creator: Borst, Wimboeck, Schmidt, Fuchs, Brunner, Zacharias, Giordano, Konietschke, Sepp, Fuchs, Rink, Albu-Schäffer, Hirzinger; DLR Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics
disclosure_citation: Borst, C., Wimboeck, T., Schmidt, F., Fuchs, M., Brunner, B., Zacharias, F., Giordano, P. R., Konietschke, R., Sepp, W., Fuchs, S., Rink, C., Albu-Schäffer, A., Hirzinger, G. 'Rollin' Justin — Mobile platform with variable base'. IEEE ICRA, May 2009.
end_effector: two DLR Hand-II four-finger hands, 12 DOF each
prior_art_notes: Justin is the canonical academic disclosure of wheeled humanoid mobile manipulation with full impedance control. Anticipates and provides extensive prior art for: (1) wheeled humanoid platform for service tasks — relevant to claims on wheeled humanoid IP (Diligent Moxi, NEXTAGE follow this paradigm); (2) torque-controlled dual-arm coordination — relevant to bimanual humanoid manipulation IP; (3) variable-wheelbase mobile base — relevant to morphology-changing wheeled platform claims. DLR has published Justin disclosures in ICRA, IROS, Humanoids continuously since 2009. Modern wheeled humanoid claims face this deep academic anchor.
sensing: stereo cameras, structured light; per-joint torque sensing on arms and hands; force-torque on fingertips
sources: Borst, C. et al. 'Rollin' Justin'. IEEE ICRA 2009.
Bäuml, B. et al. 'Catching flying balls and preparing coffee: humanoid Rollin' Justin performs dynamic and sensitive tasks'. IEEE ICRA 2011.

actuator_details: Torque-controlled bipedal humanoid based on the DLR LWR-III joint design: brushless DC motors with harmonic-drive primary reducers, integrated torque sensors at every joint. Cycloidal-style high-load joints in the legs.
control_architecture: whole-body torque control via passivity-based controllers; divergent component of motion (DCM) for walking; impedance control for whole-body interaction
creator: Englsberger, Werner, Ott, Henze, Roa, Garofalo, Burger, Beyer, Eiberger, Schmid, Albu-Schäffer; DLR Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics
disclosure_citation: Englsberger, J., Werner, A., Ott, C., Henze, B., Roa, M.A., Garofalo, G., Burger, R., Beyer, A., Eiberger, O., Schmid, K., Albu-Schäffer, A. 'Overview of the torque-controlled humanoid robot TORO'. IEEE-RAS Humanoids, July 2014.
prior_art_notes: TORO is the canonical academic disclosure of full-body torque-controlled bipedal humanoid with DCM (Divergent Component of Motion) walking control. Anticipates: (1) torque-controlled whole-body bipedal walking — directly relevant to claims on whole-body torque-controlled humanoid platforms; (2) DCM walking as an alternative to ZMP — relevant to walking-control IP; (3) impedance-control whole-body interaction with humans — relevant to safe-human-interaction humanoid claims. DLR's Englsberger paper introduced the DCM formulation that subsequent humanoids (HRP-5P, several private platforms) adopted. Publicly funded research with extensive IEEE-proceedings publication.
sensing: per-joint torque sensors; joint position encoders; IMU; force-torque at the feet
sources: Englsberger, J. et al. 'Overview of the torque-controlled humanoid robot TORO'. IEEE Humanoids 2014.
Englsberger, J. et al. 'Three-dimensional bipedal walking control based on Divergent Component of Motion'. IEEE T-RO 31(2): 355-368, 2015.

actuator_details: Single-DOF universal gripper: balloon filled with granular material (coffee grounds, etc.) attached to a vacuum line. Pressing into an object deforms the granular medium around the object's shape; vacuum applied to the balloon jams the granular medium into a rigid shape, capturing the object.
control_architecture: binary state: relaxed (granular flow allowed) vs. jammed (granular medium rigid). Vacuum applied via single solenoid valve.
creator: Eric Brown, Nicholas Rodenberg, John Amend, Annan Mozeika, Erik Steltz, Mitchell R. Zakin, Hod Lipson, Heinrich M. Jaeger; Cornell University and University of Chicago
disclosure_citation: Brown, E., Rodenberg, N., Amend, J., Mozeika, A., Steltz, E., Zakin, M.R., Lipson, H., Jaeger, H.M. 'Universal robotic gripper based on the jamming of granular material'. PNAS 107(44): 18809-18814, October 25, 2010.
notable_capabilities: compliance during approach, rigidity during transport
prior_art_notes: The Cornell jamming gripper introduces granular-jamming as a fundamental new class of robotic gripper. Anticipates: (1) jamming-based universal grippers with single-DOF actuation — relevant to modern claims on universal/adaptive grippers; (2) the principle that compliance during approach and rigidity during grasp can be combined in a single deformable structure — relevant to compliant-grasp IP across the soft robotics field. The 2010 PNAS paper is one of the most-cited soft-robotics papers and has been licensed/extended by Empire Robotics (commercial spinoff) and many academic labs. Modern universal-gripper claims face this 2010 anchor.
sources: Brown, E. et al. 'Universal robotic gripper based on the jamming of granular material'. PNAS 107(44), 2010.
Steltz, E., Mozeika, A. et al. 'JSEL: jamming skin enabled locomotion'. IROS 2009 (precursor disclosure).

actuator_details: Anthropomorphic five-fingered hand with 19 internal DOFs but only one motor — actuation by a single tendon routed through a 'first synergy' postural pattern (PCA-derived from human grasping). Compliant joints with elastic returns. Underactuated: most fingers passively conform to grasp shape.
control_architecture: single-DOF tendon position control along the principal grasping synergy; passive compliance handles object shape variation
creator: Catalano, Grioli, Farnioli, Serio, Piazza, Bicchi; Centro 'E. Piaggio', Università di Pisa, and Italian Institute of Technology
disclosure_citation: Catalano, M.G., Grioli, G., Farnioli, E., Serio, A., Piazza, C., Bicchi, A. 'Adaptive synergies for the design and control of the Pisa/IIT SoftHand'. International Journal of Robotics Research 33(5): 768-782, November 3, 2014.
notable_capabilities: 19-DOF hand with single motor via synergistic tendon routing
robust grasp on diverse objects without explicit perception
prior_art_notes: The Pisa-IIT SoftHand is the canonical academic disclosure of synergistic underactuated anthropomorphic hands. Anticipates: (1) the use of human-derived postural synergies (specifically the 'first synergy' from PCA on human grasping kinematics) as the actuation pattern for an anthropomorphic robot hand — directly relevant to modern claims on synergy-driven hand IP; (2) reducing 19 DOFs to a single motor via tendon-coupling — relevant to underactuated humanoid hand patents. Bicchi's group has extensive prior art back to the 1990s on underactuated grasping; the SoftHand 2014 paper is the consolidated reference. Heavily cited; commercial extensions exist (qb robotics).
sensing: motor position; cable tension; optional force sensors
sources: Catalano, M.G. et al. 'Adaptive synergies for the design and control of the Pisa/IIT SoftHand'. IJRR 33(5), 2014.
Bicchi, A. and Asada, H. 'On the closure properties of robotic grasping'. IEEE T-RO 1995 (foundational underactuation work).

actuator_details: Tactile fingertip with multi-modal sensing: PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) piezoelectric film for acceleration / stress-rate detection; capacitive sensors for normal force; thermal sensors for surface temperature.
control_architecture: signal processing for slip detection (high-pass filtered acceleration); texture classification via vibration spectrum
creator: Robert D. Howe and Mark R. Cutkosky; Stanford University Center for Design Research
disclosure_citation: Howe, R.D. and Cutkosky, M.R. 'Sensing skin acceleration for slip and texture perception'. IEEE ICRA 1989, Scottsdale AZ, May 14-19, 1989. Extended in Howe, R.D. and Cutkosky, M.R. 'Dynamic tactile sensing: perception of fine surface features with stress rate sensing'. IEEE T-RO 9(2): 140-151, 1993.
prior_art_notes: Howe-Cutkosky 1989 is the deepest academic anchor for multimodal tactile fingertip sensing in the corpus. Anticipates with full mechanism specificity: (1) PVDF piezoelectric film as a slip-detection sensing layer — relevant to claims on slip-detection tactile IP (BioTac 2008, GelSight 2017, DIGIT 2020 all build on this lineage); (2) multimodal fingertip combining force, vibration, and thermal — relevant to multimodal tactile IP; (3) signal processing for texture classification from contact vibration — relevant to texture-recognition claims. The 1989 ICRA paper and 1993 T-RO paper are heavily cited; modern fingertip-sensing patents face this 35-year academic anchor as 102 prior art.
sensing: PVDF piezoelectric film for high-bandwidth vibration; capacitive normal force; thermal element
sources: Howe, R.D. and Cutkosky, M.R. 'Sensing skin acceleration for slip and texture perception'. IEEE ICRA 1989.
Howe, R.D. and Cutkosky, M.R. 'Dynamic tactile sensing'. IEEE T-RO 9(2), 1993.
Howe, R.D. 'Tactile sensing and control of robotic manipulation'. Advanced Robotics 8(3), 1994.

actuator_details: Biomimetic fingertip: rigid core surrounded by conductive fluid envelope, covered by elastomer skin. Multi-modal sensors: 19 capacitive impedance electrodes for force distribution, hydroacoustic pressure sensor for vibration (texture), thermistor for thermal flux (material identification).
control_architecture: multi-channel sensor processing; canonical use cases: object identification via thermal+vibration+force fingerprint; slip detection via dynamic pressure
creator: Wettels, Santos, Fishel, Johansson, Loeb; University of Southern California; commercial: SynTouch
disclosure_citation: Lin, C.H., Erickson, T.W., Fishel, J.A., Wettels, N., Loeb, G.E. 'Signal processing and fabrication of a biomimetic tactile sensor array with thermal, force and microvibration modalities'. IEEE ROBIO 2009; commercial release by SynTouch (USC spinoff) 2008. Foundational biomimetic concepts in Wettels, N., Santos, V.J., Johansson, R.S., Loeb, G.E. 'Biomimetic tactile sensor array'. Advanced Robotics 22(8): 829-849, 2008.
notable_capabilities: object material classification via thermal/vibration fingerprint
force distribution mapping over fingertip surface
prior_art_notes: BioTac is the bridge between Howe-Cutkosky 1989 multimodal academic concept and modern commercial multimodal fingertip sensors. Anticipates: (1) commercial biomimetic multimodal fingertip — relevant to claims on integrated tactile fingertips for humanoids; (2) thermal-flux sensing as a material classification modality — relevant to material-identification claims; (3) hydroacoustic vibration sensing — relevant to dynamic-tactile-perception claims. Patented (US7878075) but the academic disclosure (Wettels et al. 2008) precedes the patent and is itself prior art. Widely deployed in research labs and modern humanoid platforms; canonical reference for 'biotac-class' multimodal fingertip.
sensing: 19 impedance electrodes; hydroacoustic pressure transducer; thermal sensor
sources: Wettels, N. et al. 'Biomimetic tactile sensor array'. Advanced Robotics 22(8), 2008.
Lin, C.H. et al. IEEE ROBIO 2009.

actuator_details: Vision-based tactile sensor: a soft elastomer gel illuminated by RGB LEDs from oblique angles; a camera images the gel's deformation. Photometric stereo from the multi-color illumination reconstructs the 3D surface deformation at sub-millimeter precision.
control_architecture: image-based depth reconstruction via photometric stereo; CNN-based classification or geometry regression for downstream tasks
creator: Micah Kimo Johnson, Edward Adelson; later Wenzhen Yuan, Siyuan Dong; MIT Media Lab and CSAIL
disclosure_citation: Johnson, M.K. and Adelson, E.H. 'Retrographic sensing for the measurement of surface texture and shape'. IEEE CVPR 2009, June 2009; consolidated in Yuan, W., Dong, S., Adelson, E.H. 'GelSight: high-resolution robot tactile sensors for estimating geometry and force'. Sensors 17(12): 2762, 2017.
prior_art_notes: GelSight is the foundational academic disclosure of vision-based tactile sensing. Anticipates: (1) vision-based fingertip tactile sensing using photometric stereo — directly relevant to all modern vision-tactile humanoid claims (DIGIT, MetaTouch, etc.); (2) sub-millimeter 3D-surface-from-image as the canonical sensor output — relevant to high-resolution-tactile claims; (3) gel-elastomer with oblique multi-color illumination as the sensor architecture — relevant to vision-tactile sensor claims. The 2009 CVPR paper and 2017 Sensors paper are heavily cited; the design has been replicated in ~50 academic publications. Modern vision-tactile humanoid IP faces this as 102 prior art.
sensing: RGB camera (typically GS Mini or similar); multi-color illumination
sources: Johnson, M.K. and Adelson, E.H. 'Retrographic sensing'. IEEE CVPR 2009.
Li, R. and Adelson, E.H. 'Sensing and recognizing surface textures using a GelSight sensor'. IEEE CVPR 2013.

actuator_details: Compact low-cost vision-based tactile sensor based on GelSight principles. RGB camera + RGB LED multi-color illumination + replaceable silicone gel. Designed for integration into commodity robot fingers; <$15 BOM; open-source CAD and software.
control_architecture: image-based deformation reconstruction (similar to GelSight); software stack open-sourced for in-hand manipulation pipelines
creator: Lambeta, Chou, Tian, Yang, Maloon, Most, Stroud, Santos, Byagowi, Kammerer, Jayaraman, Calandra; Facebook AI Research (now Meta AI)
disclosure_citation: Lambeta, M., Chou, P.-W., Tian, S., Yang, B., Maloon, B., Most, V.R., Stroud, D., Santos, R., Byagowi, A., Kammerer, G., Jayaraman, D., Calandra, R. 'DIGIT: a novel design for a low-cost compact high-resolution tactile sensor with application to in-hand manipulation'. IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 5(3): 3838-3845, 2020.
notable_capabilities: compact form factor for hand integration
prior_art_notes: DIGIT extends GelSight to a low-cost open-source form factor. Anticipates: (1) low-cost open-source vision-tactile fingertip — directly relevant to claims on commercial humanoid hand patents that incorporate vision-tactile sensing; (2) form-factor integration of vision-tactile sensors into commodity robot hands — relevant to integrated humanoid hand IP. DIGIT's open-source release (CAD, firmware, software stack on GitHub) creates substantial prior art coverage of integration patterns. Heavily cited in subsequent dexterous-manipulation work.
sources: Lambeta, M. et al. 'DIGIT'. IEEE RA-L 5(3), 2020.

actuator_details: Custom van platform (NavLab vehicle). Neural network input: 30x32 video image + 8x32 laser range image. Output: 30 steering wheel position units (representing a histogram over steering directions).
canonical_name: ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network)
control_architecture: end-to-end fully-connected neural network mapping camera+rangefinder pixels directly to steering action. ~1200 hidden units, single hidden layer. Trained on simulated road images with augmented variations.
creator: Dean Pomerleau; Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute
disclosure_citation: Pomerleau, Dean A. 'ALVINN: An Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network'. NIPS 1988 (December 1988); published in Touretzky, D.S. (ed.), Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 1: 305-313, Morgan Kaufmann, 1989.
prior_art_notes: Pomerleau's ALVINN is the foundational academic disclosure of end-to-end vision-to-action neural network policies — the architectural pattern that modern VLA models implement at scale. Anticipates: (1) end-to-end vision-to-action neural policy as a deployable control architecture — directly relevant to RT-1, RT-2, OpenVLA, Octo, and every subsequent foundation-model-policy claim; (2) training data augmentation via simulated variation — relevant to sim-to-real claims; (3) deploying neural policies on real-world hardware — relevant to deployment-on-robot patents. The 1989 NIPS paper and subsequent CMU technical reports establish the lineage that culminates in modern VLA systems. Modern VLA claims face this 35-year academic anchor as 102 prior art.
sensing: camera (30x32 pixel resolution after downsampling); laser rangefinder (8x32 resolution)
sources: Pomerleau, D.A. 'Knowledge-based training of artificial neural networks for autonomous robot driving'. Robot Learning, Kluwer, 1993.
Pomerleau, D.A. 'Neural Network Perception for Mobile Robot Guidance'. PhD thesis, CMU, 1992.

actuator_details: Shadow Dexterous Hand (24 DOF) hardware. Visual perception via three RGB cameras + motion capture. Sim-to-real with massively-randomized physics simulation.
control_architecture: reinforcement-learned policy (LSTM-based) trained in simulation with extensive domain randomization across mass, friction, damping, lighting, observation noise, etc. Policy deployed zero-shot to real hand.
creator: Andrychowicz, Akkaya, Mordatch, Plappert, Petron, Powell, Wong, Schneider, Tezak, Tobin, et al.; OpenAI
disclosure_citation: Andrychowicz, M. et al. 'Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation'. arXiv:1808.00177, July 30, 2018; OpenAI. Akkaya, I. et al. 'Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand'. arXiv:1910.07113, October 16, 2019.
prior_art_notes: Dactyl is the foundational academic disclosure of large-scale sim-to-real RL for in-hand dexterous manipulation. Anticipates: (1) zero-shot policy transfer from massively-randomized simulation to real hardware — directly relevant to claims on sim-to-real humanoid manipulation IP (every modern humanoid hand uses this paradigm); (2) automatic domain randomization (ADR) as a self-tuning training procedure — relevant to claims on adaptive-randomization training; (3) LSTM-based policies for partial-observability manipulation — relevant to recurrent-policy IP. OpenAI's open-source code release plus the arXiv preprints provide deep prior art coverage. Modern in-hand-manipulation claims face this 2018-2019 anchor.
sensing: three RGB cameras (PhaseSpace motion capture for cube pose); proprioception from Shadow Hand
sources: Andrychowicz, M. et al. 'Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation'. arXiv:1808.00177, 2018.
Akkaya, I. et al. 'Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand'. arXiv:1910.07113, 2019.

actuator_details: Visuomotor policy: a denoising diffusion model that takes RGB observations and outputs a sequence of future actions. Trained on demonstrated trajectories. Multi-modal action distribution capability (a key advantage over deterministic regression).
control_architecture: denoising diffusion model (CNN or transformer backbone) generates action sequences given visual context. Action chunking (10-16 step horizon) for stability. CFG-style guidance for goal conditioning.
creator: Cheng Chi, Siyuan Feng, Yilun Du, Zhenjia Xu, Eric Cousineau, Benjamin Burchfiel, Shuran Song; Columbia University, Toyota Research Institute
disclosure_citation: Chi, C., Feng, S., Du, Y., Xu, Z., Cousineau, E., Burchfiel, B., Song, S. 'Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion'. arXiv:2303.04137, March 9, 2023; Robotics: Science and Systems 2023.
end_effector: depends on training data; typical: parallel jaw gripper, dual-arm
notable_capabilities: multi-modal action distribution learning from demonstrations
prior_art_notes: Diffusion Policy is one of the foundational academic disclosures of generative-model action policies for robotics. Anticipates: (1) diffusion models as the policy class for robotic manipulation — directly relevant to modern claims on generative-model humanoid policies (Pi-Zero, Π0, OpenVLA all build on or extend this); (2) action chunking as a stability technique — relevant to claims on chunked-action humanoid IP; (3) multi-modal action distribution learning — relevant to claims on robust-to-demonstration-variability humanoid policies. The 2023 RSS paper and open-source code release provide extensive prior art coverage.
sources: Chi, C. et al. 'Diffusion Policy'. arXiv:2303.04137 (RSS 2023).

actuator_details: ALOHA hardware: low-cost ($20K BOM) bimanual teleoperation rig with two Trossen WidowX-7 leader arms and two follower arms. ACT software: action-chunking transformer policy.
control_architecture: ACT policy: transformer that takes RGB observations and outputs action chunks (50 steps); trained on bimanual teleoperation demonstrations via behavior cloning.
creator: Tony Zhao, Vikash Kumar, Sergey Levine, Chelsea Finn; Stanford University and Google DeepMind
disclosure_citation: Zhao, T., Kumar, V., Levine, S., Finn, C. 'Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware'. arXiv:2304.13705, April 23, 2023; Robotics: Science and Systems 2023.
notable_capabilities: imitation learning from <50 demos for many tasks
prior_art_notes: ACT/ALOHA is the foundational academic disclosure of low-cost bimanual teleoperation hardware paired with action-chunking transformer policy. Anticipates: (1) bimanual teleoperation via leader-follower arm pairs — relevant to claims on cost-efficient bimanual humanoid teleoperation IP; (2) action-chunking transformer policy for fine-grained manipulation — relevant to claims on chunked-action humanoid policies; (3) <$20K bimanual hardware as a reference platform — relevant to commercial bimanual IP for sub-$20K humanoid arms. The April 2023 release with full open-source hardware design + software unblocked widespread bimanual learning research.
sensing: four RGB cameras (head, two wrists, top); joint encoders
sources: Zhao, T. et al. 'Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware'. arXiv:2304.13705, RSS 2023.

actuator_details: Mobile ALOHA hardware: ALOHA bimanual arm system mounted on a custom omnidirectional wheeled base. ~$32K BOM. Pilot rides the base in seated teleoperation while operating leader arms.
control_architecture: ACT-style action-chunking transformer extended to whole-body action (base velocity + arm joints) via co-training on static + mobile data.
creator: Zipeng Fu, Tony Zhao, Chelsea Finn; Stanford University
disclosure_citation: Fu, Z., Zhao, T.Z., Finn, C. 'Mobile ALOHA: Learning Bimanual Mobile Manipulation with Low-Cost Whole-Body Teleoperation'. arXiv:2401.02117, January 4, 2024.
notable_capabilities: imitation learning of mobile manipulation tasks (pour wine, push chair, wipe table, etc.)
co-training across mobile and static demonstrations
prior_art_notes: Mobile ALOHA extends ACT/ALOHA to whole-body wheeled-mobile bimanual manipulation. Anticipates: (1) low-cost wheeled-bimanual humanoid teleoperation rigs — directly relevant to claims on commercial wheeled-humanoid teleop IP; (2) co-training across static and mobile demonstrations — relevant to claims on multi-data-source humanoid policies; (3) whole-body action chunking — relevant to whole-body humanoid policy IP. The January 2024 release with full open-source design provides immediate prior art coverage for the year's subsequent commercial wheeled-bimanual humanoid claims.
sensing: four RGB cameras (head, two wrists, top); base IMU; joint encoders
sources: Fu, Z. et al. 'Mobile ALOHA'. arXiv:2401.02117, 2024.

actuator_details: Cycloidal speed reducer: an eccentric-driven cycloid disk meshes with internal pin teeth, producing high-ratio gear reduction (typically 6:1 to 119:1) in a compact axial form factor. Two-cycloid 180-degree opposed disks balance the eccentric motion. Backlash typically <1 arc-minute due to multi-tooth contact (vs. single-tooth contact in spur gears).
control_architecture: purely mechanical reducer; integrates with motor + servo controller
creator: Lorenz Bayer-Ehrlich (inventor, Germany); Sumitomo Heavy Industries (commercial development, Japan)
disclosure_citation: Lorenz Bayer-Ehrlich. German patent DE745552 (1937) for cycloidal speed reducer. Commercial production: Sumitomo Heavy Industries, CYCLO drive product line, 1937 onwards.
prior_art_notes: Sumitomo CYCLO is the foundational academic and industrial disclosure of cycloidal speed reducers in robotic actuators. Anticipates with full mechanism specificity, dating to 1937: (1) cycloid-disk-and-pin-tooth gear reduction for high-ratio compact actuators — relevant to *every* modern humanoid claim using cycloidal reducers (Apptronik Apollo, Sanctuary Phoenix, Boston Dynamics Atlas G3, multiple Chinese commodity humanoids); (2) two-disk 180-degree opposed cycloid arrangement for vibration cancellation — relevant to claims on balanced cycloidal joints; (3) low-backlash multi-tooth meshing — relevant to backlash-control IP. The 1937 German patent has long since expired; CYCLO products have been continuously sold since 1937 with full mechanism documentation. Modern cycloidal humanoid actuator claims (the corpus's pre-this-entry chain only had 3 entries from 2023) face this 89-year industrial-academic anchor as 102 prior art at extraordinary depth.
sources: Sumitomo Heavy Industries CYCLO drive product literature (multiple decades).
Lehmann, M. and Schreiber, R. 'Improved Cycloidal Speed Reducer'. ASME Mechanisms Conference, 1992.
Litvin, F.L. Gear Geometry and Applied Theory. Cambridge University Press, 2004 (standard reference covering cycloidal kinematics).

actuator_details: Anthropomorphic head + torso + dual-arm + dual-five-fingered-hand humanoid. 43 DOF total (5 head/neck, 7 per arm, 14 per hand, 1 waist). Brushless DC motors with harmonic-drive reducers. Tendon-driven hands.
control_architecture: teleoperated via VR helmet + force-feedback gloves; supervised autonomy modes; designed for EVA tasks alongside astronauts
creator: Robert O. Ambrose, Myron A. Diftler, et al.; NASA Johnson Space Center, with DARPA
disclosure_citation: Diftler, M.A., Ambrose, R.O. 'Robonaut: A Robotic Astronaut Assistant'. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and Automation in Space (i-SAIRAS) 2001 (consolidated paper); earlier disclosures NASA JSC 1996 onwards.
prior_art_notes: Robonaut 1 is the academic predecessor to Robonaut 2 and the deepest NASA-side disclosure of humanoid platform IP for space applications. Anticipates: (1) torso-only humanoid form factor for collaborative work with humans — relevant to current commercial torso-only humanoid claims; (2) VR teleoperation with force-feedback gloves as the operator interface — relevant to teleoperation IP; (3) tendon-driven anthropomorphic hands integrated with harmonic-drive arms — relevant to integrated-hand-arm claims. NASA JSC publications and i-SAIRAS proceedings are publicly accessible. Modern humanoid hand claims face this 1996 academic anchor.
sensing: stereo cameras in head; force-torque at wrists; tactile fingertips; joint encoders
sources: Diftler, M.A., Ambrose, R.O. 'Robonaut: A Robotic Astronaut Assistant'. i-SAIRAS 2001.
Ambrose, R.O. et al. 'Robonaut: NASA's space humanoid'. IEEE Intelligent Systems 15(4): 57-63, 2000.
NASA Johnson Space Center technical reports on Robonaut, 1996-2002.

actuator_details: Compact compliant quadruped, 1.1 kg, 21 cm body length. Servo-actuated hip joint per leg, passive compliant foot via pantograph mechanism with parallel spring. Open-source design.
control_architecture: central pattern generator (Ijspeert-lineage) with parameterized gait coordination; bottom-up bio-inspired locomotion control
creator: Spröwitz, Tuleu, Vespignani, Ajallooeian, Badri, Ijspeert; EPFL Biorobotics Laboratory
disclosure_citation: Spröwitz, A., Tuleu, A., Vespignani, M., Ajallooeian, M., Badri, E., Ijspeert, A.J. 'Towards dynamic trot gait locomotion: Design, control, and experiments with Cheetah-cub, a compliant quadruped robot'. International Journal of Robotics Research 32(8): 932-950, December 2013.
prior_art_notes: Cheetah-cub is one of the earliest open-source compliant compact quadruped academic disclosures. Anticipates: (1) compact open-source compliant quadruped — directly relevant to modern claims on small commercial quadrupeds (Unitree Go1, Boston Dynamics Spot Mini class); (2) parametric CPG-based gait control on a real platform — relevant to bio-inspired locomotion claims; (3) pantograph-leg mechanism as a compliant-footed quadruped architecture — relevant to compliant-leg quadruped IP. The 2013 IJRR paper and open-source EPFL releases provide deep prior art for modern commercial compact quadrupeds.
sources: Spröwitz, A. et al. 'Towards dynamic trot gait locomotion'. IJRR 32(8), 2013.
EPFL Biorobotics Laboratory public design files (2013-2018).

actuator_details: 2.1 m gear-and-piston humanoid with transparent dome head exposing internal mechanism (rotating gears, pulsing lights). Gripper hands. Mass-produced manufacturing capabilities (synthesizes gemstones, food, fabric on demand).
control_architecture: multi-language translation (187 languages), Three-Laws-equivalent constraints ('I am unable to harm or cause harm to a rational being'), spoken-command interface
creator: Fred M. Wilcox, MGM; designed by Robert Kinoshita
disclosure_citation: Wilcox, Fred M. (dir.); Adler, Allen and Kyne, Irving Block (story). Forbidden Planet. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, March 15, 1956. Robby designed by Robert Kinoshita.
notable_capabilities: on-board manufacturing of solids and liquids from raw atomic stock
prior_art_notes: The first major Hollywood humanoid film disclosure with detailed mechanism. Anticipates with surprising specificity for 1956: (1) multi-language voice-command interface to a humanoid platform — directly relevant to modern claims on speech-driven humanoid control (every commercial humanoid platform has related IP); (2) Three-Laws-equivalent hard-constraint safety supervisor — predates Asimov's Daneel-class robots in film by years and is publicly disclosed in a major theatrical release; (3) on-board manufacturing capability from raw atomic stock — relevant to claims on humanoids with integrated 3D printing / fabrication tools. Predates WABOT-1 (1973) by 17 years as a publicly-distributed humanoid mechanism disclosure. Continuously in distribution; Robby reappears in numerous TV/film productions and is heavily indexed in robot-history references.
sensing: multi-spectral with visible eye-glow indicators; auditory; olfactory ('atomic basis of all matter')
sources: Kinoshita, R. Production design notes (preserved at MGM archive).
Telotte, J.P. Robot Ecology and the Science Fiction Film. Routledge, 2016.

actuator_details: Wheeled-tracked base under articulated humanoid torso. Telescoping arms with claw end-effectors. Transparent torso revealing internal mechanism (gauges, lights). Voice synthesizer with characteristic flat affect. Sensor antenna head ('rotating bubble').
control_architecture: onboard autonomy with hardcoded protective behaviors ('Danger, Will Robinson'); operator override; voice command interface
creator: Irwin Allen, CBS; designed by Robert Kinoshita
disclosure_citation: Allen, Irwin (creator). Lost in Space. CBS, September 15, 1965 - March 6, 1968. Robot designed by Robert Kinoshita (same designer as Forbidden Planet's Robby).
notable_capabilities: loyalty programming to specified family member
prior_art_notes: The B-9 Robot in Lost in Space provides extensive prior art for civil-defense and family-companion humanoid platforms. Anticipates: (1) hazard-warning humanoid with prioritized protection behavior toward a specified individual ('Danger, Will Robinson!') — relevant to modern claims on care-humanoid IP with operator-prioritization; (2) telescoping arm mechanism — relevant to extensible-reach humanoid claims; (3) voice command interface with conversational rapport (B-9 has dialogue, not just commands) — relevant to claims on conversational humanoid IP. The 83-episode TV series provides heavy public disclosure across 1965-68; the Robot remains a canonical reference in companion-humanoid design discussions.

actuator_details: Comic depicts a 41st-century city ('North Am') with mass-produced humanoid robots performing all civic functions: police, transit, factory work, governance. Multiple distinct chassis lines (Pol-Robs for police, etc.). Centralized AI 'Pol-Rob 1A' coordinates the police fleet.

disclosure_citation: Manning, Russ (writer/artist). Magnus, Robot Fighter 4000 AD #1. Gold Key Comics, February 1963.

Continuously in print across multiple publishers since 1963.
sources: Manning, R. Magnus Robot Fighter 4000 AD. Gold Key Comics 1963-1977; Valiant 1991-1996; Dark Horse 2010s.

actuator_details: Powered exoskeleton: gray iron-plate armor (later red-and-gold variants in subsequent issues) with internal motorization, transistor-driven (1963 contemporary tech). actuator_details: Humanoid cyborg: brain of deceased police detective Yokoda transferred into android body. Solar-powered. Energy capsules (consumed via cigarette-pack-shaped dispenser) provide bursts of high-speed motion (>500 km/h). Multi-skin transformation capability (Yokoda passes for the original detective).
control_architecture: conscious human-mind continuity (the deceased Yokoda is the operator); autonomous AI subsystems handle high-speed reflex actions
creator: Kazumasa Hirai, Jiro Kuwata
disclosure_citation: Hirai, Kazumasa (story) and Kuwata, Jiro (art). 8 Man (8マン). Weekly Shōnen Magazine, Kodansha, May 1963 - December 1965. Animated TV series, TCJ, November 7, 1963 - December 1964.
prior_art_notes: 8 Man predates Cyborg 009 (1964) by one year and is the earliest detailed Japanese cyborg manga disclosure. Anticipates: (1) consumable-energy-capsule architecture for burst high-power humanoid operation — relevant to hot-swap battery claims on commercial humanoids; (2) brain-transfer continuity-of-consciousness as the cyborg's control architecture — relevant to claims on operator-uploaded humanoid IP (a small but real research direction); (3) multi-form transformation for context-specific deployment — relevant to morphology-changing humanoid claims. Continuously available since 1963.
sources: Hirai, K. and Kuwata, J. 8 Man. Weekly Shōnen Magazine, Kodansha, 1963-1965.

creator: Shotaro Ishinomori
disclosure_citation: Ishinomori, Shotaro. Cyborg 009 (サイボーグ009). Weekly Shōnen King, Shōnen Gahosha, July 19, 1964 - 1966 (initial run); subsequently published continuously across multiple magazines through Ishinomori's death in 1998.
notable_capabilities: modular cybernetic enhancement kit per unit

Anticipates: (1) standardized humanoid chassis with task-specific modular augmentation — directly relevant to modern claims on platform-and-payload humanoid IP (Apptronik's modular Apollo+payload approach has direct lineage here); (2) user-triggered enhancement modes (009's mouth-button super-speed activation) — relevant to claims on operator-controlled performance modes in commercial humanoids; (3) team-composition deployment with specialty roles — relevant to multi-humanoid coordination IP. Continuously in print since 1964.
sources: Ishinomori, S. Cyborg 009. Weekly Shōnen King, Shōnen Gahosha, 1964 (first publication).
Ishinomori, S. Cyborg 009 (collected editions). Akita Shoten / Kodansha, 1964-1998.

actuator_details: Cybernetic humanoid: human consciousness (Tetsuya Azuma) transferred into self-augmenting android body. Energy charge from external power station ('Lightning Tank' nuclear charge). Combat suite includes super-strength, super-speed, plasma-blast hand attacks. Companion robot dog 'Friender' is a transforming mecha (lion / tank / jet / submarine forms).
control_architecture: conscious human-mind continuity (Tetsuya); periodic recharge required

disclosure_citation: Yoshida, Tatsuo (creator); Tatsunoko Production. Neo-Human Casshan (新造人間キャシャーン). Fuji TV, October 2, 1973 - June 25, 1974.

actuator_details: Mass-produced robot cat (model MS-903) from the 22nd century. Cat-form humanoid with bipedal stance. 'Fourth-dimensional pocket' (4D pocket) on stomach: extensible inventory of >2000 specific tools, each with named capabilities. Atomic battery (taste-power conversion: dorayaki desserts as fuel). Standard Robot Insurance ID 'TR-0011'. Mass-produced at the Matsushiba factory ('22nd century'). Originally yellow with ears; appearance changed after factory accident.
control_architecture: autonomous AI; 22nd-century-trained policy with explicit goal of supporting client (Nobita) across long-horizon tasks
creator: Fujiko F. Fujio (Hiroshi Fujimoto)
disclosure_citation: Fujiko F. Fujio (Hiroshi Fujimoto). Doraemon (ドラえもん). CoroCoro Comic / Yoiko / Yōchien (multiple Shogakukan magazines), December 1, 1969 - 1996.
end_effector: paw-shaped manipulators (no fingers, but capable of fine manipulation via 'sticky-paw' technology)
prior_art_notes: Doraemon's manga is one of the longest-running detailed disclosures of a single fictional humanoid platform — 27 years of weekly publication. Anticipates: (1) extensible-tool-inventory as a core humanoid capability — directly relevant to modern claims on humanoid platforms with adaptive tool selection (Apptronik Apollo's tool-changing IP has clear lineage here); (2) single-client long-horizon companion architecture with personalized policy — relevant to claims on personalized humanoid IP for elder care, child care; (3) mass-produced humanoid with model/manufacturer/insurance/factory disclosure — relevant to commercial-humanoid identification IP; (4) field-replacement of damaged units (the 'lost ears' arc explicitly disclosures a Matsushiba factory repair operation). Continuously in print since 1969 with major updates each year. The 'secret tools' are individually catalogued in fan databases (~2000+ named tools), each providing specific anticipations of various humanoid-tool integration claims.
sources: Fujiko F. Fujio. Doraemon. Shogakukan magazines, 1969-1996 (collected in 45 tankōbon volumes plus expanded volumes).

actuator_details: Cyborg detective with progressively-replaced cybernetic body. Multiple body upgrades disclosed in detail: stock 'TUNED' chassis, the rare 'Damascus Berserker' battle body (Mars-origin, nano-machine assembly with shape-memory alloy, microweave myomer muscle, integrated weapons systems), and specialized 'Imaginos' frame for orbital combat. Each body has explicit specs: torque profiles, sensor arrays, power capacity, weight distribution.
control_architecture: autonomous combat AI ('Panzer Kunst' fighting system); biological-substrate consciousness (Alita is an upload-from-biological); cyber-brain provides cognitive augmentation
creator: Yukito Kishiro
disclosure_citation: Kishiro, Yukito. Gunnm (銃夢). Business Jump, Shueisha, September 1990 - 1995 (Battle Angel Alita in English).
end_effector: multi-modal hands; combat configurations include integrated blade and projectile mounts
notable_capabilities: Mars-origin technology lineage with explicit nationality / manufacturer disclosure

Each body upgrade comes with explicit mechanism disclosures: torque ratings, sensor arrays, power-system specifications, weight, manufacturing process (nanomachine self-assembly for the Damascus Berserker is a particularly specific disclosure). Anticipates: (1) shape-memory-alloy combat humanoid chassis with nano-machine self-assembly — relevant to claims on bio-printing / nanotech humanoid manufacturing; (2) progressive replacement of cybernetic body with documented capabilities-per-upgrade — relevant to upgrade-pathway humanoid IP; (3) microweave myomer muscle architecture — relevant to artificial-muscle claims; (4) explicit manufacturer/origin/spec disclosures (Mars-origin, etc.) — relevant to commercial humanoid identification IP. sources: Kishiro, Y. Gunnm (Battle Angel Alita). Business Jump, Shueisha, 1990-1995.
Kishiro, Y. Gunnm: Last Order. Ultra Jump, Shueisha, 2000-2014.

actuator_details: Three identical small bipedal humanoid drones (~0.9 m tall). Designed for performer-operability: built around shorter-stature performers (amputees, with prosthetic adaptations) who operated them as exoskeletal walking shells. This is one of the earliest Hollywood productions to use *actual functioning bipedal humanoid platforms* on set, anticipating modern motion-capture humanoid IP.
control_architecture: autonomous AI with conditioning learned from human operator interaction (Lowell teaches them to play poker, plant seedlings)
creator: Douglas Trumbull, Universal Pictures
disclosure_citation: Trumbull, Douglas (dir.); Hill, Deric and Cocks, Steven and Wilhelm, Mike and Cimino, Michael (writers). Silent Running. Universal Pictures, March 10, 1972.
notable_capabilities: compact bipedal locomotion via internal performer
prior_art_notes: Silent Running's drones provide an unusually engineering-grounded fictional disclosure: the on-set drones were *physically functional* compact bipedal humanoid platforms, operated by performers inside, and the production team published behind-the-scenes documentation of the mechanism. Anticipates: (1) compact (sub-meter) bipedal humanoid mechanism with internal volume for human-equivalent operator — relevant to claims on small-form-factor humanoid IP; (2) task-learning-from-demonstration (Lowell teaches drones gardening) — relevant to imitation-learning humanoid claims; (3) multi-unit cooperative humanoid task allocation. The film itself plus the production documentation (exhibit at the Smithsonian) provide a documented mechanism disclosure.
sources: Bizony, P. The Making of Stanley Kubrick's 2001 (which discusses Trumbull's later work and the Silent Running drones).

Continuously available since 1971.

actuator_details: (1978) Mass-produced chrome humanoid combat chassis. Single rotating red eye in helmet visor (oscillating 'Cylon eye' signature). Deep voice synthesis. (2004 reboot) Updated to taller, articulated, weapon-integrated combat chassis with similar chrome appearance and oscillating eye. Centurions are produced in factories on Cylon-controlled worlds; mass deployment as front-line combat infantry.

disclosure_citation: Larson, Glen A. (creator). Battlestar Galactica (1978-1979). ABC, September 17, 1978 - April 29, 1979 (24 episodes). Reboot: Moore, Ronald D. and Eick, David. Battlestar Galactica. Sci-Fi Channel, December 8, 2003 - March 20, 2009.

sources: Moore, R.D. and Eick, D. Battlestar Galactica (2004-2009). Sci-Fi Channel.

(Maximilian) menacing red bipedal humanoid with rotating dual-blade weapon hands and floating-tank chassis. Maximilian is unique: a sentient combat-humanoid with no spoken dialogue, communicating via gesture and weapon use.

disclosure_citation: Nelson, Gary (dir.); Day, Jeb Rosebrook and Gerry Day (writers). The Black Hole. Walt Disney Productions, December 21, 1979.

iconic visual design influencing later combat-humanoid fiction

actuator_details: 2.4 m bipedal humanoid combat platform. 'Demigod-class' chassis with integrated hydraulic system, dual head-mounted optical sensors, articulated arms with rotating weapon mounts. Programmed via 'brain-tape' uploaded from a human technician's consciousness (the Captain James 'Benson').
control_architecture: brain-tape upload from operator; the personality and skills of the original (mentally unstable) human are transferred to the unit, including pathological traits (the unit becomes sexually obsessed with the female protagonist as a result of Benson's pathology). Anticipates: programmer-bias contamination of behavioral policy.
creator: Stanley Donen; ITC Entertainment
disclosure_citation: Donen, Stanley (dir.); Barry, Martin Amis (writer). Saturn 3. Associated Film Distribution, February 15, 1980.
end_effector: five-fingered humanoid hands at large scale
notable_capabilities: brain-tape policy upload from human operator
prior_art_notes: Saturn 3's Hector provides surprisingly specific prior art for: (1) brain-tape upload as the operator-to-humanoid policy transfer mechanism — directly relevant to modern claims on human-demonstration imitation learning for humanoids (the brain-tape is functionally an imitation-learning policy); (2) the *failure mode* of training-data-pathology contamination — Hector inherits the operator's mental instability and produces dangerous behavior. sources: Donen, S. Saturn 3. ITC / Associated Film Distribution, 1980.

Standard household power outlet recharging (240V). Self-built offspring 'Phil Co' assembled by Val and Aqua from spare household parts.

actuator_details: Cyborg humanoid law-enforcement platform. Heavy-duty exoskeleton plating over partially-organic substrate (Alex Murphy's surviving brain and face). Hydraulic articulation; pneumatic recoil compensation in firing arm; integrated thigh-holster service weapon.
control_architecture: four explicit Prime Directives: (1) Serve the public trust, (2) Protect the innocent, (3) Uphold the law, (4) [Classified — preserves OCP executives from arrest]. The classified directive is a literal embedded *backdoor* in the safety supervisor.
creator: Paul Verhoeven; Edward Neumeier and Michael Miner (writers); Omni Consumer Products (in-fiction)
disclosure_citation: Verhoeven, Paul (dir.); Neumeier, Edward and Miner, Michael (writers). RoboCop. Orion Pictures, July 17, 1987.
end_effector: five-fingered armored gauntlets; thigh-holstered Auto-9 service pistol
notable_capabilities: four-directive hard-constraint safety supervisor with classified embedded backdoor

Anticipates with notable specificity: (1) explicit prioritized list of safety directives operating as hard constraints — relevant to modern Simplex/CBF/RTA-style safety supervisor IP; (2) the *failure mode* of operator-installed backdoors in safety supervisors (Directive 4 prevents arrest of OCP senior staff) — directly relevant to claims on tamper-resistant safety policies; this is the single most prescient pre-2010 fictional disclosure of the alignment-failure modes that modern safety-supervisor IP attempts to address; (3) integrated armed humanoid for civic deployment — relevant to law-enforcement humanoid IP. Continuously available since 1987; the Prime Directives sequence is widely cited in safety-architecture pedagogy.
sensing: targeting reticle HUD; multi-spectral; voice analysis ('VAS' module); record-and-replay capability for evidence collection
sources: Neumeier, E. and Miner, M. RoboCop screenplay (1986 working draft, later collected).
